items.title: Newton's biggest theorem says integration and differentiation are inverses
items.claim: Define F(x) as the area under f from 0 to x. The derivative of F is f. Define G(x) as an antiderivative of f. Then integral from a to b of f dx = G(b) - G(a). Two operations that look unrelated are inverses.

options.text: Integration (continuous summation) and differentiation (instantaneous rate) seem like different operations — but they undo each other. This is one of the most surprising and powerful results in mathematics

items.reveal:
Two parts:

FTC Part I: If f is continuous on [a, b] and F(x) = integral from a to x of f(t) dt, then F is differentiable on (a, b) and F'(x) = f(x).

FTC Part II: If f is continuous on [a, b] and G is any antiderivative of f (so G'(x) = f(x)), then integral from a to b of f(x) dx = G(b) - G(a).

Geometric intuition for Part I: F(x) is area under the curve up to x. As x increases by a small amount dx, the area increases by approximately f(x) * dx — the height at x times the width dx. So dF/dx = f(x).

Why it's surprising:
- Differentiation computes a LOCAL rate at one point.
- Integration sums up TOTAL accumulated value across a range.
- The connection: knowing the total at every point tells you the rate; knowing the rate everywhere tells you the total.

Applications:
- Definite integrals become easy: find an antiderivative, plug in endpoints, subtract.
- Areas, volumes, work, charge, total amounts of accumulated quantities — all computable via antiderivatives.
- Differential equations: solving f' = g is equivalent to finding an antiderivative of g.

Historical: Newton (~1665) and Leibniz (~1675) both discovered it independently. It's the cornerstone of mathematical physics.

Before the FTC, calculating areas under curves (the 'quadrature problem') was a major mathematical challenge — Archimedes computed parabola areas through laborious limit arguments. After the FTC, antiderivatives reduce the problem to algebra.
items.why: Calculus has two halves that look unrelated. The fundamental theorem reveals they are inverses — the same way logarithm and exponential are inverses. This unification is the most powerful idea in elementary mathematics.

items.title: Half the world's billionaires got there partly by luck
items.claim: Repeated coin flips produce some very lucky streaks. The proportion of 'successful' (still in business, in market, alive) entities at the top of a population sample is dominated by selection effects — the unsuccessful disappear from view, leaving the survivors looking exceptional.

options.text: Survivorship bias: we only see the successes, and infer skill from outcomes; randomness alone would have produced some 'winners' from a starting pool, but we don't see the matching losers

items.reveal_title: Survivorship bias and the law of large pools
items.reveal:
If 10,000 hedge fund managers each pick stocks randomly for 10 years, about (1/1024) * 10,000 ≈ 10 will have called the market right 10 years running (by pure luck). These 10 will be on the cover of business magazines, will publish books on their 'secrets', and will attract investor billions.

The other 9,990 are out of business and forgotten.

Mochon and Norton (2011, 2012) replicated this in the lab: random stock-picking among 'subjects' produced 'expert' track records statistically indistinguishable from actual hedge funds. Selection of survivors creates the illusion of skill.

Real-world cases:
- WWII US bombers: aircraft returning from missions had bullet holes in wings and fuselage, not engines or cockpits. The Air Force initially considered reinforcing where the holes were — until Abraham Wald pointed out: planes hit in the engine or cockpit don't return. Reinforce the unhit areas.
- Famous 'success stories' (Steve Jobs, Bill Gates, J.K. Rowling) tell entrepreneurs what to do — but tens of thousands who tried the same things failed.
- Stock market: survivor-bias-corrected returns are ~1-2% per year lower than uncorrected indices, because failed stocks drop out.

The correct statistical question is not 'what did successful X do?' but 'what's the base rate of success among everyone who tried that?'.
items.why: Success seems instructive. Survivorship bias means we systematically learn from outliers and ignore the (invisible) ordinary cases. The math of selection effects is more important than the stories of any individual.

items.title: 1 is the first digit of natural numbers 30% of the time
items.claim: Take any 'natural' set of numbers — house prices, river lengths, populations, physical constants. Look at the first digit. About 30% start with 1. Only 4.6% start with 9. The pattern is so reliable that auditors use it to detect fraud.

options.text: Benford's law: for scale-invariant distributions, the probability of first digit d is log10(1 + 1/d). The math reflects that doubling a number (or scaling by any factor) takes longer to pass through 1-2 than through 8-9 on a logarithmic axis

items.reveal:
Simon Newcomb (1881) noticed that the early pages of his logarithm tables (corresponding to leading digit 1) were more worn than the later pages. He inferred something about how often various leading digits appeared.

Frank Benford (1938, physicist) systematically tested the rule across many datasets (river lengths, populations, atomic weights, baseball stats, addresses). He found:
Digit 1: 30.1%
Digit 2: 17.6%
Digit 3: 12.5%
Digit 4: 9.7%
Digit 5: 7.9%
Digit 6: 6.7%
Digit 7: 5.8%
Digit 8: 5.1%
Digit 9: 4.6%
Formula: P(d) = log10(1 + 1/d).

Why: many natural quantities span multiple orders of magnitude. On a logarithmic scale, the spacing from 1 to 2 (log 2 ≈ 0.30) is much wider than from 9 to 10 (log 10/9 ≈ 0.046). If the distribution is roughly uniform in log space, leading digits follow Benford.

Applications:
- Forensic accounting: real financial data follow Benford; fabricated numbers usually don't. Auditors flag tax returns or financial statements that deviate.
- Election fraud detection: ballot counts in honest elections follow Benford; many disputed elections have shown deviations.
- Scientific fraud detection: many cases of data fabrication caught.
- Image authenticity: pixel JPEG coefficients follow Benford-like distributions; fakes often don't.

Limitations: Benford requires scale-invariant data spanning multiple orders of magnitude. Constrained data (height, ages) don't satisfy it. Carefully fabricated data designed to fool Benford also exist.

The mathematical generalisation: any distribution with logarithmic density invariant under scaling will produce Benford's law for leading digits.
items.why: Random-looking data often follow precise patterns. Benford's law is counterintuitive and has practical applications in fraud detection. It's also a window into how scale-invariance shapes the structure of numbers we encounter.
